claims.text: Eutectic high-entropy alloys with dual-phase lamellae can serve as a transition material between diffusion-mediated and dislocation-mediated creep.
The intrinsic microstructure of dual-phase EHEAs allows control over interface coherency.
An EHEA multilayer can possess highly coherent lamellar interfaces formed during synthesis.
HPHT processing can form highly coherent lamellar interfaces in an EHEA multilayer.
Changing HPHT treatment parameters can gradually reduce interface coherency.
Both diffusion-mediated and dislocation-mediated creep may be active at elevated temperatures under sub-critical to moderate applied stresses.
Interface coherency at lamellar phase boundaries is the structural variable mediating creep behavior in dual-phase EHEAs.
Highly coherent interfaces cause grain-boundary or interface diffusion to dominate creep.
Reducing interface coherency introduces misfit or semi-coherent interfaces.
Misfit or semi-coherent interfaces make dislocation nucleation and glide easier.
Loss of interface coherency shifts the dominant creep mechanism from diffusion-mediated creep to dislocation-mediated creep.
At lower temperatures and high interface coherency, creep exhibits a stronger diffusion-controlled rate.
At higher temperatures or after controlled loss of coherency, dislocation-mediated creep contributes more significantly.
A change in the dominant creep mechanism will alter creep rate and its stress dependence.
As-formed EHEA multilayers with highly coherent dual-phase lamellae exhibit predominantly diffusion-mediated creep.
The mechanism transition occurs at a critical combination of temperature, stress, and interface coherency.
The temperature, stress, and coherence thresholds for the proposed transition are not well constrained.
